title: Vintage Menus Are a Glimpse into the Golden Age of Dining
summary:
Eugen Beer and Barbara McMahon aim to preserve dining culture through their enormous collection of vintage menus.

The post Vintage Menus Are a Glimpse into the Golden Age of Dining appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
In 2012, Eugen Beer, a British publicist, and Barbara McMahon, a Scottish journalist, were working on a project at home in the U.K. While searching through the University of Nevada’s online archives, they came across an old menu from Café Anglais in Paris, which closed in 1913. It featured a little boy feeding a piece of meat to the moon

“We were just completely charmed,” Beer says. “It opened a giant rabbit hole for us.”

The couple became engrossed in a world of menu collectors, archivists, and dealers they never knew existed. More than a decade later, they’ve pored over thousands of menus pulled from cardboard boxes and library shelves across the U.S.

They’ve found hand-painted cards from late-19th-century New York banquets, keepsakes from the golden age of cruise liners, and mid-century masterpieces made for Hawaiian hotels. They’ve unearthed forgotten commercial work by Saul Bass and Paul Rand, two of the 20th century’s most influential graphic designers. They even found a menu from 1947 that William Steig—the creator of Shrek—designed for Welton’s in Worcester, Massachusetts, listing Cognac at 75 cents.

Today, Beer and McMahon run the business Vintage Menu Art, selling menu prints from their ever-growing, 1,500-strong catalog. But if you ask Beer, the commercial appeal is almost beside the point. It’s more about their passion for preserving dining culture. “It’s a slice of Americana that Americans forgot,” he says.

Dining at restaurants became a part of American life just before the turn of the 20th century. As manifest destiny led Americans westward, cities sprang up across the heartland, creating new demand for hotels, restaurants, and bars.

“There was no dining-out culture in the U.K.—except for the very rich—until the ’60s,” Beer explains. “But in the U.S., whenever a place like Dodge City emerged, one of the first things they did was establish a hotel and import a bartender from the East Coast.”

Then, after Prohibition, restaurants boomed nationwide, and their owners began commissioning artists to make their menus stand out in an increasingly crowded field.

“The food at that time was all the same. It was steak, it was lobster, it was burgers,” Beer says. Whether it was promoting the zombie cocktail in Waikiki or the art of enjoying wine, the menus were a colorful form of marketing that helped turn ordinary meals into nights to remember.

In retrospect, they also reveal how restaurants kept drinks cheap to compete with other spots.

“Immediately after Prohibition, in 99% of places, cocktails would have started at 25 cents,” Beer says. “We have one menu from Tail o’ the Cock in the 1940s. The most expensive dish, a filet mignon, was $4.95, and a bottle of Château Margaux was $5.75.”

The U.S. was fertile ground for menu hunting for another reason: Americans held onto them. For generations, people kept menus tucked into scrapbooks, a practice Beer attributes to both rising purchasing power and a distinctly American appetite for souvenirs.

The golden age of menu design flew under the radar for decades, but some of them eventually found their way into private and institutional collections. By the early 2010s, the Culinary Institute of America in New York alone had up to nearly 50,000 menus. Getting access to them was surprisingly difficult, though.

“At the New York Public Library, you’d have to book an appointment. You could only see two menus at a time,” Beer says.

Private collectors offered another way in. One was Henry Voigt, a former DuPont executive who started buying menus at auctions in the 1990s and eventually amassed more than 10,000. Beer considers him one of the foremost custodians of American menu art, and he agreed to let the couple work with his collection.

Ever since, Voigt has been a key inspiration and resource for Vintage Menu Art, which sells prints from his collection. Voigt has also donated more than 2,600 pre-20th-century menus to the American Antiquarian Society. Voigt would say he’s simply preserving “the history of everyday life.”

“[These menus] not only reflect what the people were eating but also what they were doing and what they valued—the symbolism of food,” Voigt tells me.

He says a menu can transport you to a moment in history, like one in his collection from Springfield, Massachusetts, dated April 16, 1865, the day after Abraham Lincoln’s assassination. Its black border looked like a printing error at first. Then Voigt realized it was printed that way to mourn the president’s death.

“You put yourself in that dining room,” he says, “and through dinner, you’re hearing church bells all over Springfield because they rang all day that Sunday.”

For Beer and McMahon, rescuing forgotten menus is a labor of love. First, they scour auctions and follow leads for unique pieces. “We don’t care if it comes from Poughkeepsie or Punxsutawney. Does the menu speak to us?” Beer says of their search criteria.

Those that make the cut are scanned and cleaned up, pixel by pixel, removing creases, stains, and other damage. They also research the stories behind the designs, packing as much history as they can into each reproduction, including original menus, prices, and all. Then, they print them on archival paper and sell them online, at their permanent booth in L.A.’s Farmers Market, and at art and wine fairs on the West Coast.

Now, between museums and commercial print sales, these menus are reaching new audiences again. Beer says they still achieve what their creators intended.

“These were designed to entertain, to make people anticipate a nice time, and they’re still doing that,” he says. “When people pick up a print [at our stall in L.A.], they go, ‘Wow, have you seen this?’ They whip themselves up into a frenzy of excitement.”

title: These Italian Wine Family Dynasties Have Been Reigning for Centuries
summary:
Through centuries of upheaval in the Italian wine world, these five families have endured and become icons of perseverance.

The post These Italian Wine Family Dynasties Have Been Reigning for Centuries appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Hold tight to tradition, study the past, respect your elders: These are the rules in Italy. Legacies are meant to be maintained, and ostensibly nowhere does this matter more than in the wine business.

But a deep history can also be a mirage. Take, for example, the so-called “Carbonaragate” scandal. A decade ago, a French website published a bad carbonara recipe video. In lieu of the traditional preparation—pork cheek and pecorino quickly tossed with tempered egg yolk over spaghetti or bucatini—it used onion, bacon, bowtie pasta, and crème fraîche, boiled together in a pot, then topped with a raw egg.

A rage-fueled media frenzy started in Italy and spread around the world. It was more than just a miserable execution of a classic Roman pasta dish; what Italians really couldn’t forgive was the audacity of someone assaulting the timehonored, immutable foundations of their cuisine.

The irony is that carbonara has only been around since maybe the end of World War II. Though the idea of Italian identity dates back to the Roman Empire, Italy didn’t exist as a unified country until 1861 and didn’t start exporting a singular “Italian” cuisine until around 75 years ago. Most of the Italian food staples the world knows are relatively new.

There are a few exceptions, like the holy trinity of bread, olive oil, and wine. Wine has been produced on the peninsula for thousands of years, perhaps longer. That said, the Italian wine we drink today is, in many ways, very young—the vines, the land, and the people who work them have changed so much over the past few decades.

After the creation of the European Economic Community in 1957, open trade across the continent encouraged regions with extended growing seasons and fertile terrain—especially Italy, particularly in the south—to shoot for quantity over quality. Wineries then sold their grape must to less blessed agricultural areas, where achieving phenolic maturity and a high alcohol content were constant challenges. Super juice from southern Italy was used to pump up their final product.

In 1964, the sharecropping system that had sustained most of Italy’s agrarian estates for centuries started to dissolve. This led many multi-generation winemaking families to sell their land or convert it to other purposes. By the 1970s, Italy was still producing far too much grape must, so the government incentivized families to destroy their vineyards, and many thousands of hectares of old vines were ripped out.

All this means that, much like carbonara, most Italian vineyards can’t claim to be continuous commercial estates that predate the mid-20th century. Many celebrated Italian winemaking families today have made wine for themselves or their immediate community for generations, some going back to the Middle Ages. But very few have been operating professionally that entire time, making the same wine, from the same land, with the same people, for more than a few decades. Here are five iconic Italian wine families that have stood tall while withstanding these transformations and challenges—and are now absolutely towering.

Pio Cesare

When Cesare Pio founded his winery in 1881, the nation of Italy was still in its infancy. Pio’s passport was one of the first issued by the new country—number 55—and remains in the family’s archives. He can be credited with setting the foundation for a future that would ultimately see the wines of Piedmont become some of the most celebrated in the entire world.

In the 19th century, Cesare Pio identified the unique terrain in the Langhe that could maximize the potential of their native grape and bring to life an exceptional Piedmontese wine. But Nebbiolo, finicky in the vineyard and austere in the bottle, was not necessarily suited to changing trends. At Pio Cesare, attention has been given to shaping Barolos and Barbarescos that carry the weight of their history while offering increasingly accessible elegance.

Managing Director Federica Boffa, who is in the fifth generation of the Pio-Boffa family, knows she has her work cut out for her. “We understand that it is a BIG [emphasis hers] responsibility connected not only to our family but also to our city, our region, our appellation, and our terroir,” she says. “Climate is definitely not helping us in making this task easier, not guaranteeing we will still be able to grow Nebbiolo in the future with the same authentic expression of the past.”

She also knows that the more people drink these wines today, the more likely she is to guarantee Pio Cesare’s success tomorrow. “Barolo and Barbaresco are very democratic wines, not to be presented only in a jacket and tie, but also in jeans and a T-shirt,” she says. To do this, Boffa tries to employ a more informal approach in all senses: using simpler language, pairing the wine with many different cuisines, and presenting it not only in formal dining venues but also in relaxed bars and cafés. She insists that history shouldn’t make Barolo feel challenging, but should instead add to its appeal, making it more “cool, fun to enjoy,” not less.

Boffa’s democratic approach to wine reflects changes in social politics that extend far beyond the cellar. If at one time making Barolo feel exclusive and elite was a means of lifting it out of obscurity, now an inclusive, expansive approach will allow it to spread its wings.

Pio Cesare 2022 Bricco di Treiso “Il Bricco” Nebbiolo (Barbaresco)

From the highest plots of Bricco di Treiso, Il Bricco has carried the clear voice of this vineyard since 1974, and a difficult vintage has done nothing to quiet it. Warmed cherry compote, crushed strawberries and dried herbs finely worked together offer a savory, uplifting complexity. The palate answers with generous baked plum and raspberry, tannins open and welcoming now but very much built to travel. Drink now to 2040. Cellar Selection. 95 Points — Jeff Porter

Inquire with the winery

Tenuta San Leonardo

San Leonardo is a storied estate in northeast Italy’s Trentino region. Reflecting on the moment he took over, Marchese Anselmo Guerrieri Gonzaga recalls, “When my father passed me the responsibility for San Leonardo, he asked me to ‘take care of it.’” Simple words, but deadly serious ones if you’re about to take the reins of vineyards that have been in your family for 300 years.

Indeed, there was no question what his father meant by taking care of this place—keeping things the way they had always been. “One lesson I was taught was to remain completely faithful to the past and to be very conservative about change,” Guerrieri Gonzaga says.

But being a custodian of your family’s legacy often means finding solutions to future threats. While San Leonardo was known for just one wine—a spectacular Cabernet Franc-forward blend often ranked among the world’s greatest—Guerrieri Gonzaga intuited a need to meet the moment, and that meant new grape varieties.

“I felt we needed to bring San Leonardo to a wider audience and show that we could create wines for different occasions,” he says. “This gave the estate new energy and allowed more people to discover our work, while keeping San Leonardo at the center of everything.”

The introduction of a cru Carménère and white wines has changed their production substantially, but their practice stays the same. The new wines have also allowed the San Leonardo team to show the breadth of their talents.

Paraphrasing the famous lines from the Sicilian aristocrat Giuseppe Tomaso di Lampedusa—who observed that in order for everything to stay the same, everything must change— Guerrieri Gonzaga says, “I wanted to preserve what my father created, while allowing the estate to grow. Perhaps what I discarded was the idea that being faithful to the past means keeping everything exactly as it was.”

Tenuta San Leonardo 2024 Vette Sauvignon Blanc (Vigneti delle Dolomiti)

Like hiking through an alpine meadow with a basket of citrus. The freshness hits different here, more crystalline than crisp. This is the wine equivalent of that perfect summer day when everything just feels right. Grilled shrimp would make it even better. 91 Points — J.P.

$23 Liquor Pantry

Marchesi Antinori

In the Italian wine world, there may be quibbles over the length of a family’s legacy, but one name ends all arguments. Giovanni di Piero Antinori joined the guild of winemakers in Florence in 1385, and his successors have made wine ever since in their home territory of Tuscany.

Many of their iconic bottles have both created and then transcended the trends that have defined global wine-consumption patterns. From its beating heart in Chianti Classico, the Antinori family network stretches out to Montalcino and Bolgheri, and then well beyond to Puglia, Piedmont, and Franciacorta. Recent years have only seen their presence explode further in the U.S., with the acquisition of Napa Valley’s Stag’s Leap and Washington’s Col Solare.

To say that Marchese Piero Antinori has a lot of history to carry is an understatement. He has learned to be agile in both diversifying holdings and facilitating the passage of so much responsibility. His daughter, Albiera, is now the president of the company, with her sisters Allegra and Alessia serving as vice presidents. In his current role as honorary president, Piero can now appreciate that change is inevitable, often to the benefit of legacy. “In the 24 generations that preceded me, the rule was that only sons should run the business,” Piero says. “In my case, for the first time, I did not follow this rule. Having only daughters, I had no choice. I am glad to say that, considering the results, I consider this change a positive development.”

Marchesi Antinori 2021 Buiano Castellina Gran Selezione Sangiovese (Chianti Classico)

The nose is earthy and floral, with aromas of top soil, tulips and cherries, plus a bit of chocolate for nuance. The palate brings an intensity and layering of flavors that makes you sit up and pay attention, as an umami earthiness emerges first, then high notes of sweet cherries, and finally a finish where that hint of chocolate from the nose takes over. 96 Points — Danielle Callegari

$145 Zachys

Emidio Pepe

Emidio Pepe bottles have become cult objects because they are pure expressions of the earth. They became sought-after wines following the 1960s, when Emidio Pepe first took steps to engage with sustainable, regenerative farming and low-intervention winemaking, becoming part of a revolution that later metamorphosed into the natural wine movement of today.

But the Pepe family should be given its due when it comes to longevity debates. They’ve made wine without interruption on this land since 1889, when it was called Casa Pepe. That’s no small feat anywhere on the peninsula, and even more impressive in Abruzzo, long dominated by co-operatives and still dogged today by a reputation for making more grape juice than great labels.

Emidio Pepe passed away this summer after 94 magnificent years of living and breathing wine, but his work continues in the capable hands of his granddaughter, Chiara De Iulis Pepe. Yet to arrive at the age Dante called the midpoint of our lives (35), Chiara is already an internationally acclaimed winemaker steering the Pepe ship with a vision that’s making waves well beyond the Adriatic. “I have to keep doing things that are a little bit weird, a little bizarre,” she says, “because that’s what defines this place.”

While change and growth are her constants, she perceives tradition as antithetical to stagnation. “[Tradition] is not something you carry like a backpack or a heavy burden,” she says, “it’s something that you’re a part of. You have to see tradition through a dynamic lens, in which things are moving.”

Her grandfather planted pillars for her, as she describes it, but there’s plenty of room for her to dance in the space between them. That freedom to move keeps her limber enough to hold those pillars high.

Emidio Pepe 2022 Montepulciano (Abruzzo)

A very umami, savory nose of pepper, earth, hot tar, crushed rocks and old leather is balanced out by a palate that presents tart berries and lots of citrus, beneath a sprinkle of salt and pepper. The finish unveils a spiced, bitter cocoa element, wrapping up a wine which is layered, dense and substantial, but also agile, directed and linear. 95 Points — D.C.

$150 K&L Wine Merchants

Tasca d’Almerita

Wineries in southern Italy were the most likely to be uprooted by the 20th century’s seismic upheavals. So the fact that the Tasca family’s flagship estate, Tenuta Regaleali, remains firmly grounded on 550 hectares in the middle of Sicily is nothing short of a miracle.

Even more surprising, the property hasn’t changed hands, or much else, since 1830. The vineyards are still dedicated to a mixture of native Sicilian grapes and international varietals, crafted into wines that seem earthquake-proof—safely attached to their foundation, but with built-in flexibility that allows them to bend in a new direction without breaking. The eighth generation is now preparing to take over the estate, along with four other properties that have been added to their roster over the years, allowing them to vastly expand their global reach.

If Alessandro Tasca is nervous about the shoes he has to fill, he mostly takes it in stride. “What scares me most is probably also one of the best parts of the job: working with my family,” says Alessandro, who is preparing for a leadership role in the future. “Being part of a family business is special because you are building something together with the people closest to you. At the same time, that is exactly what can make it difficult. Business relationships and family relationships do not always remain separate, and disagreements at work can easily become personal.”

With a lot of cooks in the kitchen, things can get hot quickly. Tasca takes the long view and decentralizes himself to get perspective: “My role is not simply to inherit what previous generations built, but to protect it, improve it, and eventually pass it on to the next generation. Thinking this way helps me remember that the legacy is bigger than any one person.”

Tasca d’Almerita 2020 Tenuta Regaleali Nozze d’Oro White Blend (Sicilia)

Melon, pear, apple and a hint of white peach are on the nose. The palate is juicy with more pear and melon, with the sweet, slight astringency of candied lemon peel and a welcome salty note, like licking a rock. 92 Points — D.C.

title: The Best Mezcals of 2026 to Gift (or Keep for Yourself)
summary:
WE Writer-at-Large Kara Newman shares the year’s best mezcals to sip or stir into cocktails—including one with a perfect 100-point score.

The post The Best Mezcals of 2026 to Gift (or Keep for Yourself) appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
In an age where mezcal bars are plentiful and the Mezcal Old Fashioned is considered a modern classic, it’s hard to believe that just a few years ago, few Americans knew about this Mexican liquor distilled from agave. 

Today, mezcal is firmly in the mainstream, and as popular as its cousin tequila, also made from agave. They belong to one of the few spirits categories that continues to see growth. According to the Distilled Spirits Council of the United States, tequila and mezcal sales totaled $6.4 billion in 2025, which places the category right behind vodka, the longtime market leader.

A key reason for its continued popularity: mezcal offers plenty of discovery opportunities for curious agave fans. Compared to tequila, made with a single cultivar of agave (Blue Weber) within one of five regions in Mexico, mezcal can be made from more than 20 agave species—Espadin is the best-known—within nine Mexican states. No wonder mezcal offers such a diverse array of expressions, from citrusy and crisp to smoky and savory. And to clear up an oft-cited stereotype: No, not all mezcals are smoky.

Furthermore, not all mezcals are clearly labeled as “mezcal.” For a spirit to be officially certified as such, producers must pay a fee, and many of them opt to skip the cost. Instead, their products are classified as Destilados de Agave (literally “distillates of agave,” or “agave spirits”).

Many of those spirits are excellent: a destilado de agave by Cazcanes, a Jalisco-based producer of small-batch spirits, earned a perfect 100-point score from one of our critics. The Cazcanes Destilado de Agave Nuestras Raices Still Strength Blanco is a wild and expressive spirit that unfolded bell pepper, jalapeño, lime peel, and crumbled sage, plus a surprising hint of cacao.

In the years to come, mezcal will most likely continue to command attention. Consumers—particularly younger audiences—are increasingly choosing drinks that are authentic, bear a sense of place, and tell a story, and a lot of mezcal fits the bill. Here are a few of our favorite mezcals of 2026.

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

El Silencio Mezcal Rare

This complex mezcal unfolds salinity and tropical funk, resulting in sea breeze-y, aged cheese-y, and lightly fruity flavors. Ripe banana, lychee, rosewater, and a hint of almond sweetness linger into a lip-smacking finish dotted with pink peppercorn and sea salt. Made with espadin and bicuishe y barril agaves. 97 Points — K.N.

$187 Lost N Liquor

Rosaluna Mezcal

Made with single estate-grown espadin agave, this mezcal has a bold dried oregano scent. The palate shows jalapeno, graphite, and dried herbs, finishing with a sooty exhale and black pepper heat. 93 Points — K.N.

$32 Total Wine

Dady’O Mezcal

This espadin has a lightly smoky scent. On the palate, that campfire smoke quality mixes with tinges of dark chocolate and sea salt, plus a roasty, warming finish. Best Buy. 93 Points — K.N.

$50 Keg N Bottle

Los Perdidos De La Noche Tepeztate Mezcal Reposado

Four months of aging in casks that previously held Cognac lend a pale straw hue to this mezcal, made with tepeztate agave. The first sips lead with jalapeno and graphite, softening into banana tinged with vanilla. The drying exhale is warmed with a flurry of black pepper plus a hint of anise. 92 Points — K.N.

$200 Blackwell’s Wine and Spirits

Mocel Mezcal Artesanal Ensamble

Herbaceous, zesty and complex, this ensemble mezcal (made with a blend of agave varieties) opens with lively, mouthwatering lime peel, lemongrass and pine, winding into rosemary and tarragon midpalate. The long exhale finishes with cubeb pepper and pink peppercorn snap. Limited edition of 582 bottles. 95 Points — K.N.

$232 Tipxy

Cazcanes Destilado de Agave Nuestras Raices Still Strength Blanco

Note: this is not certified as a tequila nor mezcal, it’s a destilado de agave (agave distillate). Nomenclature be damned – this is an exquisite spirit. It’s downright kaleidoscopic, by turns citrusy, vegetal, lightly spiced, ever-changing from one sip to the next. But if it must be pinned down: expect a zesty aroma and a lively, complex, bold flavor. Tons of bell pepper and jalapeno, lime, and surprising hint of cacao give way to an extraordinarily long finish showing crumbled sage, slivers of lime peel, and ginger root, extinguished by a final cayenne flicker. This is one to sip and share. 2025 Special Edition. Nuestras Raices means “our roots.” 100 Points — K.N.

title: How Did These Ancient Varietals Wind Up in California?
summary:
Golden State winemakers are connecting to their heritage by planting indigenous grapes like Vranac, Koshu, and more.

The post How Did These Ancient Varietals Wind Up in California? appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Michelle Sakazaki never imagined that making wine in the Napa Valley would have anything to do with her family’s Japanese roots.

In 2018, the Sacramento-born, Tokyo-raised former fashion designer who runs Kazumi Wines learned that the nursery at UC Davis was growing Koshu grapes. Though long assumed to have been brought straight from Europe to Japan by sea during the colonial era, recent studies have revealed that Koshu is a blend of Vitis vinifera and wild East Asian vines that arrived on the archipelago much earlier.

“They believe it came from the Caucasus through the Silk Road to China,” Sakazaki said. The bright pink grape was traditionally only eaten in Japan until the late 1800s, when it was first used to make wine. “I’d had it a few times in Japan,” said Sakazaki, “but I didn’t think much of it.”

Her dad was far more intrigued by the UC Davis vines, and drove to the university’s Foundation Plant Services, or FPS, to check them out. Born in Japan but raised in California, Jack Sakazaki spent 40 years running a sports-marketing agency back in Japan. He retired to Napa, quickly grew bored, and, in 2009, launched the 90 Plus Wine Club for Asian wine buyers. That’s what lured Michelle into the wine industry, and they started buying Koshu canes and propagating them in 2019.

“He somehow convinced two growers in Napa to plant this unknown Japanese variety on their properties,” said Michelle. “My dad is the best salesman ever.”

Seven years later, the Sakazakis have spread Koshu across eight acres in Northern California—two vineyards in Napa Valley and a newer planting in Lodi. “As far as we know, it’s the first commercially planted Koshu in the country,” said Michelle, who now makes 1,000 cases of still white and 250 cases of sparkling Koshu, with 100 more in extended tirage, dwarfing the less than 200 cases she makes of Sauv Blanc, Cab, and Pinot Noir. “The Koshu is our flagship right now,” she said.

The Sakazakis’ project is just one example of modern vintners connecting to their heritage by planting ancient grapevine varieties from their homelands. Of course, generations of American winemakers of French, Italian, Spanish, and Portuguese origins have done this, as so many varieties first grown here came from the Old World. But it’s more challenging to find, import, and be the first to cultivate varieties from wine regions that aren’t as internationally pervasive: places from Austria’s Wachau region to Armenia’s Vayots Dzor, from the Greek islands to the Balkan Mountains, and, yes, even Japan.

While these nascent efforts are certainly heartwarming to those involved, they could also benefit the American wine scene at large. At a time when consumers are seeking something special, these deeply personal wines bring new flavors and stories to the table. And as vintners grapple with the curious effects of climate change, these varieties may just serve as strategic tools of survival.

From the Balkans to Paso

When Rick Quinn co-founded Opolo Vineyards in Paso Robles in 1999, the original strategy was to promote his Balkan background. “Opolo,” after all, is the name for a rosé wine from the Dalmatian Coast. With grandparents from Herzegovina and Montenegro, Quinn grew up surrounded by Balkan culture in Duluth, Minnesota, where so many from the eastern Mediterranean came to work in the steel mills.

Quinn found success as a realtor north of Los Angeles and, like generations before him, made wine at home every year. That passion led him to plant vineyards in Paso Robles and then open his tasting room in 2001.

“We started serving Balkan food like whole barbecued lamb—no one up here was doing that,” said Quinn. “We thought we could build a community around that.”

Every year, he hosts a massive, two-night harvest party for 700 people, roasting more than two dozen lambs, serving more than 2,000 cabbage rolls, and featuring Croatian singers and Serbian dancers. “It’s like My Big Fat Greek Wedding on steroids,” laughed Quinn. “That’s the only way I can explain it.”

He was one of the first California wineries to take fans on cruises, and surely the first to take them to the Balkans. It was during those trips that Quinn started wondering whether they could plant the region’s leading red grape, Vranac, in Paso Robles.

“The literal translation of Vranac is ‘black stallion,’” said Quinn. “It’s oblong like Primitivo, and it’s darker than Petite Sirah, which is where it gets its name.”

UC Davis originally acquired a Vranac clone in 1971, but it wasn’t released to the public until 2018, the same year the first 1,000 vines were planted at Opolo. But Quinn had to register Vranac with the U.S. government, as no one had bottled the wine here before. That took more than a year of patience, but the Vranac was an immediate hit. Opolo now grows three acres and produces about 300 cases of Vranac annually, all of which sell out quickly, even though customers are limited to two bottles each.

“It’s never going to be a workhorse,” said Quinn. “But people are surprised because it’s a different wine for California.”

Special Delivery From Crete

Not far away from Opolo is Boutz Cellars, where father and son James and Manoli Boutzoukas wanted to pay homage to their family village of Ano Meros on the Greek island of Crete. But they weren’t content with just one grape. They’re now growing five combined acres of seven varieties: the Greek grapes Assyrtiko, Xinomavro, Moschofilero, and Agiorgitiko, as well as the rare Cretan varieties of Vidiano, Liatiko, and Kotsifali.

A longtime wine lover—and home winemaker—the elder Boutzoukas originally bought a Paso property to serve as a retirement home and vacation rental. But with his son prepared to handle the farming, the project “just kind of unfolded,” said James, and now they have more than 52 acres planted in two vineyards, mostly with the Rhône and Bordeaux varieties common to the area.

“I thought it would be very cool to see how the varieties from our village in Crete would do here in America,” said James, noting that the latitude is exactly the same as in Paso Robles. “We have the same diurnal shifts in Crete; it could be 105 degrees in the daytime and 62 degrees at night.”

So far, only the Greek white varieties have yielded enough fruit to make wine, but the results have been stunning. Wine from the red grapes Agiorgitiko and Xinomavro is in the barrel, and they may even explore more varieties next year, like Mandilari and a clone of Thrapsathiri, both of which are indigenous to Crete.

James is most hopeful for the Liatiko, as they imported around 20 cuttings from his grandfather’s village in Crete and shepherded it through the UC Davis process. “We are super excited to be able to have that,” said James, noting that red can be made in a light or dark style. “That was the gateway to our interest in planting the other grapes.”

A Rare Armenian Grape in San Luis Obispo

Down the coast near San Luis Obispo, Ryan Deovlet of Deovlet Wines sits in a self-imposed limbo. He pays UC Davis’s FPS annually for exclusive access to the nursery’s Areni Noir vines but has so far been unable to find the right place to plant them. The variety hails from Armenia, which his grandfather escaped in 1914 just before the genocide. Dewey Diran Deovletian eventually became a metal fabricator in Los Angeles, and dropped the “-ian” from their family name in the 1940s to help his business.

Deovlet first heard about Areni Noir about a decade ago, and then learned that it was already at FPS, brought to winemaker Tony Kooyumjian in the United States by renowned Armenian vintner Vahe Keushguerian from the Vayots Dzor region. Kooyumjian’s plan to grow it in Missouri didn’t work out, so he gave control—and that annual bill— to Deovlet three years ago.

“I started thinking how incredible it would be when bottling my Areni Noir to add the ‘-ian’ back to my surname on that particular label,” said Deovlet, who thinks about his grandfather’s life a lot. “He’s my inspiration when I’m dragging during harvest: Suck it up! You’re a winemaker on the Central Coast. It’s not that bad. As tired as you think you are, you didn’t escape a genocide.”

As Deovlet tries to find a home for the Areni, other vintners without Armenian ties are itching to plant the variety as well. “I don’t mean to be a hoarder, but I respect Tony and Vahe’s effort to get it here,” said Deovlet, who wants to make sure the variety is treated with respect. “I’d like to be the first.”

What the Homeland Tastes Like in California

Michelle Sakazaki on Koshu: “It’s kinda like Pinot Gris. It’s pink during the growing season, but by the time we pick it, it’s almost red. It has this umami character that goes well with Japanese cuisine.”

Rick Quinn on Vranac: “Darker than Petite Sirah, which is where it gets its name, black stallion. It’s a huge wine, but it has some fruit that comes through.”

James Boutzoukas on Liatiko: “It can be black, rosé, or light and fresh. And then there are guys who age it 10 years.”

Ryan Deovlet on Areni Noir: “Pinot Noir meets Sangiovese meets Grenache meets Gamay.”

Grüner Takes Root in Los Olivos

Anna deLaski grew up in Austria’s Wachau region, where Grüner Veltliner reigns supreme. “I grew up hiking through the vineyards and ending up at a heuriger [wine tavern],” recalled deLaski. “That was my connection to wine.”

On her honeymoon in 2011, she and her music producer husband, David deLaski, drove from Los Angeles to the Edna Valley, where they tasted a Grüner by Zocker, one of the first producers in California to grow the variety. “It was really surprising that Grüner would grow here,” Anna said, and they decided to make one barrel of Grüner just for fun. “That was the beginning of Solminer.”

The barrel eventually became a wine company and a five-acre vineyard in Los Olivos, where they now grow Grüner, Riesling, Muscat (a.k.a. Gelber Muskateller in Austria), Blaufränkisch, St. Laurent, and Syrah. “In the tasting room we promote Austrian varieties every day,” Anna said. “That’s me giving back to my motherland.”

As one of the loudest proponents of regenerative and biodynamic farming in the region, Anna recognizes a much higher purpose for these varieties. “Here, typically French grapes are grown, but diversity is what makes our region special,” Anna said. “I’m grateful that the more obscure grapes are getting a little bit of attention. With climate change, resilience comes from having a lot of different grapes.”

Back in Napa, Koshu offers a similar hope. “This is a grape that will withstand heat and ripen slowly and not lose its acidity. Koshu could be a grape for the future,” said Kazumi’s Michelle Sakazaki. “I feel like it was meant to be, like I was supposed to meet this varietal. It’s an honor to be the first in the United States to make it.”

title: An Iconic Wine Region Is in Trouble. These Families Are Fighting to Save It
summary:
Against all odds and financial prudence, winemakers have been revitalizing the Mosel's forgotten vineyards.

The post An Iconic Wine Region Is in Trouble. These Families Are Fighting to Save It appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Despite Riesling’s enduring cachet, the Mosel is on the brink of disaster. A financial storm is battering thousands of grower estates along its meandering banks. Costs have skyrocketed, wine is in surplus, and consumer demand is shrinking.

Matthias Knebel of Weingut Knebel said it costs him an average of $14.32 a liter to farm his terraced vineyards, while U.S. importers paid an average of $3.81 per bottle of German wine. When I asked Philip Lardot of Lardot winery if his expenses were similar, he shot back, “He’s a brave man for doing that calculation. No one wants to do it.”

Devastatingly, many vineyards here are now worthless. Abandoning them leads to hefty fines. Ripping them out, while expensive, laborious, and heartbreaking, is the only option.

Vineyard land in the Mosel declined by 1% in 2024 and 2% in 2025. That doesn’t sound like much, but it’s not just the amount lost that matters; it’s the type of vineyards. They are usually steep, terraced, and own-rooted, many with 50- to 100-year-old vines. These ancient sites with genetically diverse, resilient vines have been worked by hand for thousands of years and are a precious part of winemaking history.

The 1971 German Wine Law significantly expanded vineyard land by allowing flatter areas into the appellation. Flat vineyards aren’t predisposed to low-quality wines, but planting non-Riesling varietals, pumping them full of fertilizer, and cropping five times as much as on steep sites dilutes the Mosel signature. A region whose reputation was built on its steepness is now around 60% flat or gently sloping. Vineyards expanded to 12,509 acres by 1989 before taking a nosedive in the ’90s. Today, vineyard acreage is about 65% of its peak.

All that’s the bad news. The good news is that brave winemakers are taking big swings to restore the vineyard sites.

Andreas Adam of Weingut AJ Adam has revived the fortunes of several Grosse Lage (essentially Grand Cru) Mosel vineyards. Winemaking skipped a generation in his family, and at only 18 years old, he took up the mantle, starting with a few parcels from his grandparents in the village of Dhron, where not a single vintner remained.

His sister, Barbara, joined him in 2013, and now they farm 6.7 hectares, notably the renowned Dhroner Hofberg and Häs’chen vineyards. Like other successful estates, Adam is offered vineyards to purchase every week, but he can no longer afford to say yes.

Julian and Nadine Haart of Weingut Julian Haart both hail from Mosel winemaking families. Based in Piesport, with the famed Goldtröpfchen vineyard looming above their cozy home, they could have simply farmed an assortment of its parcels and lived easier lives. Instead, Julian’s pursuit of perfection led him to revive once-forgotten sites like Schubertslay and Wintricher Ohligsberg. In Julian’s deft hands, they are once again producing some of the most sought-after wines in Germany.

But even for the Haarts, the struggle of farming Schubertslay was too much. It’s so steep and hard to work, especially organically, that it requires hundreds of hours of labor a year, with ultralow yields in return. Unable to turn a profit, they arranged an unconventional swap with a friend, the legendary Klaus Peter Keller of Weingut Keller. The deal was Schubertslay in return for parcels in Rheinhessen, which, for the Haarts, are an insurance policy against climate change. But even Keller, one of the few German winemakers who can demand the price that Schubertslay requires, has decided to give it up when the lease ends.

Now Julian and Nadine are focused on trading up in quality. “We want to give back some basic vines and find another [vineyard] that is better,” Nadine said.

In 2022, when Rosalie Curtin joined Philip Lardot at his burgeoning Mosel winery, Lardot, he had 1.7 hectares of vines. They were sold out of everything before it was bottled and looking to expand. “We put an ad in the local newspaper [and] within 36 hours, we got calls offering more than 10 hectares,” Rosalie said. “Most of them for next to nothing or free.”

Both are transplants, she from Minnesota and he from Holland by way of Finland. He moved to the Mosel over a decade ago, smitten by the grapes. After farming in the Sierra Foothills with dreams of making wine in the Jura, Rosalie responded to a job posting to work for Philip. She, too, was smitten by the grapes—and also by Philip. They were married in their Zeller Domherrenberg vineyard last year.

All of their vineyards are scattered throughout several villages on tiny parcels, mostly in hard-to-reach places. Unlike the locals, who are tied to a single village or the one next door, the Lardots have the luxury of diversity from a swath of incredible sites. Their penchant for natural wines has freed them from the staunch traditions of the Mosel, namely its off-dry prädikat designations, to the chagrin of the natives.

A few years ago, the Lardots were eyeing the single-staked, healthy-vined terraces above their prized Sankt Aldegunder Himmelreich vineyard. They were hoping the owners would hold on for a while, so they could save up more. But when their neighbors, whose family had been making wine since the 1500s, announced, “We’re quitting. You take it, or it gets ripped out,” it was now or never. Now the Lardots lease the vineyard for free; in the 1990s, the average price to lease land in the area was $1,480 per hectare.

“Looking at our parcels in general,” Philip said, “they would have been worth multiple millions just 40 years ago.”

Then orders shrank, terrible weather in 2024 wiped out most of their fruit, and they had to let their only employee go. When asked why they bother making wine in the Mosel, Rosalie cheekily responded, “Have you seen the vineyards? They’re ungrafted vines and beautiful, historic vineyards.”

With no government intervention, the onus of preserving the sites falls on these families. There simply aren’t enough willing workers, domestic or imported, to do all the vineyard work by hand. There is a sharp edge to the slow death of the Mosel that cuts a little deeper: It’s knowing that humans have invested so much in these sites for millennia, in a place of profound, hushed beauty that produces wines of radiant magnificence.

What can be done to change the fortunes of the Mosel? Andreas Adam hopes the next generation will mix things up. “We would be really happy to have some younger people who like to continue here with steep vineyards, or maybe to mix it, not only wine growing,” he said. “When I look back at my grandparents, it was mixed farming. Maybe we can go back to this again. It’s not so easy, I know.”

title: The Best European Ski Destinations for Really Good Wine
summary:
In these Alpine destinations, there’s more to après ski than Cristal and caviar.

The post The Best European Ski Destinations for Really Good Wine appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
A ski trip gives you plenty to plan beyond the slopes. When should the gang take a break? Where should you stop for lunch? And, perhaps most crucially, which bottles deserve a place at dinner? 

Across the Alps, the answers range from mountain huts pouring natural wine to hotels with extraordinary cellars. Some resorts also put you within reach of vineyards ripe for tours and tastings. From France to Slovenia, these seven destinations make room for both good skiing and good wine.

Chamonix

France

If steep terrain is your priority, follow New York wine importer and avid skier Zev Rovine to Chamonix, his favorite place to ski in the Alps. For a mountain lunch, he recommends the rustic Refuge Chalet de Lognan, which offers sweeping views from atop Grands Montets mountain. “The food is simple and perfect, and they usually even have a natural wine or two,” Rovine says.

When choosing a bottle, explore Savoie through its crisp Jacquère, floral Altesse, and peppery Mondeuse, all good companions to Alpine cooking. For a vineyard detour, head to Domaine des Albatros in Chignin. Founded in 2023 on family land, the estate stretches from steep mountainsides to the gentler ground of the Combe de Savoie, growing all three alongside Roussanne, Petite Arvine, and Gamay.

Courmayeur

Italy

Across Mont Blanc from Chamonix, Courmayeur offers scenic intermediate runs and challenging off-piste terrain, with a local wine culture rooted in high-altitude vineyards and distinctive Alpine grapes like Prié Blanc and Fumin. When making your plans to visit, Rovine recommends building in lunch at Chiecco, a wooden chalet restaurant at Plan Chécrouit. He calls it “one of the best on mountain restaurants I’ve ever been to,” praising its extensive wine list and hearty regional dishes, such as polenta made from organic stone-ground cornmeal, homemade pasta and Fassona beef.

For a break from the slopes, head down the valley to family-run estate Ermes Pavese in Morgex. Book a tasting to explore its still and sparkling wines made from Prié Blanc, the local white grape cultivated on low pergolas beneath Mont Blanc.

Valais

Switzerland

Valais offers skiing beneath the Matterhorn in Zermatt and on the sunny slopes of Crans-Montana, with vineyards lining the Rhône Valley below. Regional specialties include citrusy Petite Arvine, textured Heida, and dark-fruited Cornalin.

In Zermatt, Zurich restaurateur Patrick Schindler recommends The Rex, “a down-to-earth hotel with thoughtfully curated food and wine menus.” Head to its restaurant Stockhorn for wood-fire cooking (grilled lamb cutlets and pork belly with teriyaki are highlights) or downstairs to Weinzeit for natural wines from small growers.

For a vineyard visit, pair skiing in Crans-Montana with a tasting at Cave Caloz in nearby Miège. With terraced vineyards overlooking the Rhône Valley, the family’s organic estate welcomes visitors by appointment, with cellar and vineyard tours available on request.

Gstaad

Switzerland

For a picturesque Swiss getaway, Gstaad’s surrounding ski areas suit travelers who enjoy scenic cruising, although the steep Tiger Run on Wasserngrat gives experienced skiers a challenge. When it’s time to eat, Schindler recommends the elegant La Bagatelle at Hotel Le Grand Chalet. “They offer an amazing range of wines, from big brands to artisanal producers, for all budgets,” he says.

Hotel director Pedro Ferreira curates the cellar, which accompanies seasonal French and regional cooking. Ask about Swiss bottles, including Chasselas from Vaud or Pinot Noir from the Lake Biel vineyards in the canton of Bern. Both offer a regional connection, though vineyard visits require a separate excursion from Gstaad.

Lech

Austria

Lech’s groomed pistes and powder terrain connect into the sprawling Ski Arlberg domain. Its wine appeal is equally extensive, with standout hotel cellars like Rote Wand, especially interesting for natural wine lovers, and Almhof Schneider in the area.

Austria’s main vineyards lie farther east, but local lists provide an introduction to the country. Try Grüner Veltliner and Riesling from Lower Austria, Blaufränkisch from Burgenland, or Sauvignon Blanc from Styria.

For a casual glass, head to Sandhof Wine Bar, in an eponymous hotel with apartments and chalets. One of the bar’s developers, Clemens Riedl, says, “The goal was high quality, low barrier. Everybody is welcome.”

Riedl also leads Weinberg Arlberg, an early-winter wine symposium featuring tastings, discussions and dinners with winemakers and wine experts, gathering guests from all over the world. Plan a visit around the event, scheduled for December 3 to 13 this year, to give your ski holiday a more substantial wine itinerary.

Alta Badia

Italy

Alta Badia’s wide, groomed pistes and Sellaronda connections make it a strong choice for intermediate skiers. The warmer vineyard valleys of South Tyrol supply crisp Pinot Bianco, fragrant Gewürztraminer, light-bodied Schiava, and firmer Lagrein.

Myrtha Zierock, part of the family-owned winery Agricola Foradori, says, “One of the real food-and-wine engines in Alta Badia is Ciasa Salares.” Its owner Jan Clemens Wieser, whom Zierock describes as “a freestyle skier who really lives his village and mountains,” has made wine an essential part of the hotel’s experience. Book a meal at Cocun, its intimate cellar restaurant, and dine on venison tartare with blueberries and mountain pine while surrounded by roughly 24,000 bottles on display.

On the slopes, Wieser recommends Rifugio Col Alt for “elevated comfort food with a great wine selection” and Rifugio Punta Trieste, a welcoming hut built from old barn wood at 2,200 meters. At neighboring wine bar Ursus Ladinicus, the family pairs hearty mountain cooking with an extensive wine selection.

Kranjska Gora

Slovenia

If you haven’t considered Slovenia for a ski vacation, it’s time you do. Kranjska Gora’s approachable slopes suit beginners and families, while nearby Podkoren offers tougher racing terrain. Neighboring Planica is famous for its ski-flying competitions, where the world’s best soar off the giant hill. Make your base beside Lake Jasna, at Milka. This boutique hotel offers rooms and ski packages, plus a breakfast of specialty coffee, sourdough bread, granola, fruit, local cheeses and charcuterie (including bear salami), and smoked fish that ranks among the best I’ve had in my life.

“Milka is perhaps the most ambitious restaurant project in Slovenia,” says Slovenian food journalist Kaja Sajovic, who praises its local ingredients, menu with “a hint of New Nordic,” and “carefully curated wine list.” Chef David Žefran’s Alpine-inspired tasting menu deserves an evening of its own. Explore small Slovenian growers through Rebula from Brda, the Vipava Valley’s Zelen, or Vitovska from Kras. Visiting vineyards in those areas means a scenic road trip, but Milka brings Slovenia’s wine diversity to the table after a day on the slopes.

title: American Wine Legend Merry Edwards Changed California Pinot Noir Forever
summary:
Over five decades, Edwards has earned widespread acclaim as a pioneering winemaker, leaving a lasting impression on Sonoma County and beyond.

The post American Wine Legend Merry Edwards Changed California Pinot Noir Forever appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Wine Enthusiast’s 2026 American Wine Legend is one of the most influential figures in California wine history. Over five decades, Merry Edwards has earned widespread acclaim as a pioneering winemaker, leaving a lasting impression on Sonoma County and beyond.

One of the first female winemakers in California, Edwards cut her teeth at Mount Eden Vineyards in the Santa Cruz Mountains in the 1970s, when the industry was in a period of profound growth and experimentation. 

California wine hadn’t blown up yet. While there was some understanding of what grew well and where, our modern appellation map had yet to take shape. Even at this early stage, Edwards became intensely focused on Pinot Noir, especially the differences among the various clones. This fascination would eventually lead her to isolate a clone from Mount Eden that’s now known as UCD 37, or, more familiarly, the Merry Edwards Selection. 

When Edwards moved to Sonoma County to become the winemaker at the then-new Matanzas Creek Winery in the late ’70s, her focus began to sharpen. Living in Sebastopol, in the heart of the Russian River Valley, she recognized that the area was the place for her to craft the type of wines she intuitively knew were possible in California. 

In 1996, after refining her craft for almost 20 years, Edwards purchased the site of what would become the Meredith Estate vineyard. The next year, she founded her own brand, Merry Edwards Winery and Vineyards. The wines that Edwards bottled under this new label became benchmarks for age-worthy California Pinot Noir. Her wines were celebrated in the press and were a hit at restaurants all over the country, helping cement the reputation of the Russian River Valley as a standard bearer for Pinot Noir. 

Perhaps most importantly, Edwards’ influence on wine culture isn’t just in the bottle. Her legacy lives on in the generations of women who have followed in her footsteps, as well as the success of all the winemakers she mentored. Heidi von der Mehden, Greg Brewer, Christine Benz, Jeff Stewart, Julia Iantosca, and Greg La Follette all learned their craft under the guidance of this legend. 

“Today, I can reflect on my years in the wine business and feel that I truly contributed and had an impact on people and on winegrowing philosophy and techniques,” Edwards says. “I am proud of what I achieved, and thankful that I had the drive and dedication to do what I set out to do and provide others with some guidance along the way.”

While Edwards retired in 2020, her label lives on under the ownership of Maison Louis Roederer, with Heidi von der Mehden crafting exceptional wines in Edwards’ signature style.

title: The Secret to a Good Marriage? A Really Good Birthday Party
summary:
Paul Greenberg has been throwing his wife elaborate birthday parties for decades. It’s the secret to their marital success.

The post The Secret to a Good Marriage? A Really Good Birthday Party appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
What brings two people together is a very specific chemistry.

What keeps them together is a much more mysterious alchemy.

For Esther and me, the core of that alchemy is our birthdays, or, rather, the fact that we had always felt hurt about the day we were born right up until the day we found each other. My birthday is July 4. Esther’s is December 26. Everyone leaves town on the Fourth. On the day of Esther’s nativity, Jesus still takes the cake. That we were both latchkey kids in families broken by Me Generation divorces made our special days feel very un-special. If we got ice cream and a candle, we considered ourselves feted.

So, early in our coupledom, I realized elevating her birthday was key. I determined that Esther’s birthday deserved its own word altogether. The word I coined was EstFest.

Now, planning EstFest is tricky. How Esther wants to celebrate must arise from her own thought process. Were I to suggest “Steak frîtes and Burgundy!” the answer would be “non!” But one year, when I mentioned that a very Siberian December was coming and that something from a cold country might fit the bill, she replied, “Vodka! Borscht!” That year we celebrated “Est-ski Fest-ski” with caviar and blini, herring, and black bread. Our heads and those of the 30-odd friends at the party had Stolichnaya-sized headaches on December 27. Still, everyone gave it an emphatic “da!” and called for a repeat.

So, did we do Est-ski Fest-ski part two the next year? No, of course not.

As we all know from Annie Hall, “a relationship is like a shark. It has to constantly move forward or it dies.” There can be no EstFest repeats.

Following Est-ski Fest-ski, the brilliant author Darra Goldstein sent me her magnificent Nordic cookbook, Fire and Ice. Knowing EstFest was approaching, I left the book out for Esther to discover during one of her night-owl dissertation-writing sessions, steering her wishes in a Nordic direction. From that, “Esten Festen” was born.

By chance, our quirky neighborhood liquor store hosted an Aquavit tasting, and we were quickly hooked on that bracing northern firewater. Deducing, too, that Nordic food is just this side of Slavic, I managed in Brighton Beach, Brooklyn, to find the ingredients for all the dishes, including a sprat-based casserole called Jansson’s Temptation. There were too many dishes, too much drink, resulting in too many aching heads. Still, I counted Esten Festen another success.

Soon, the 20th EstFest beckoned. This, I knew, would be a tall order. It had to be special. And yet, somehow I knew what EstFest XX would be before she suggested it. Many years ago, when our son was an infant, we managed a rare date night that began, as these things do, with a terrible argument. I have no recollection of what the fight was about, only that when we reached the restaurant, there was talk of telling the babysitter we were headed home. Then came wine and oysters. Six superb Peconics paired with a bracing Chenin Blanc. The argument evaporated. Two more glasses came. “What argument?” we asked ourselves at meal’s end. Ever since, we have regarded oysters and wine as a source of harmony in our relationship.

So, this year when Esther suggested oysters, my only questions were “how many?” and “which wines?” I wrote to Chris Quartuccio at the Blue Island Oyster Company on Long Island’s Great South Bay. He said the day after Christmas was the best time to get oysters sent to New York City. And just like that, 50 Pink Moons, 50 Hampton Bays, 50 Blue Islands, and 50 Wellfleets were on their way.

Meanwhile, I sent an email to Eric Ripert at New York’s legendary Le Bernardin, hoping to get that busy man’s attention for wine suggestions. Soon enough, my email pinged with oyster-loving Ripert’s picks:

  • Champagne: Guiborat NV Téthys Blanc de Blancs Grand Cru Extra Brut
  • Muscadet: Pépière 2023 Sèvre et Maine sur Lie “La Pépie”
  • Chablis: Domaine Testut 2023 Côte de Bréchain

But how the hell was I going to open 200 oysters? That’s when the greatest miracle of all occurred. Turns out, the 19 previous EstFests had not only strengthened my partnership with Esther but had also built an enduring communal love for the EstFest concept. It was no sweat to recruit eager shuckers from the list of invitees. One friend had worked at a fish market in his youth and arrived ready for action, wearing long blue rubber gloves.

Just before the rest of the crowd arrived, I opened the Blanc de Blancs and poured it for the shell-spackled shucking crew. Esther, her dark eyes flashing, her face still unlined and youthful even after earning a midlife doctorate, raising a son, and enduring me and everything else New York could throw at her, happily clinked glasses with our friends.

Hemingway wrote in his memoir A Moveable Feast that when he paired oysters and wine, he “lost the empty feeling and began to be happy and to make plans.” I felt the same after EstFest XX.

Twenty years have flown by, and there are still so many more EstFests to plan.

title: From Sweet to Bone-Dry: How to Choose the Best Riesling for Your Palate
summary:
Different styles of Riesling are made around the world. Here are some helpful tips to find your perfect bottle.

The post From Sweet to Bone-Dry: How to Choose the Best Riesling for Your Palate appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
On March 13, 1435, a cellar ledger in Germany’s Hessische Bergstrasse recorded the purchase of six Riesslingen vines. This is now celebrated as Riesling’s official birthday. 

In the centuries that followed, the grape became the pride of German viticulture. By the late 19th century, its finest bottles fetched prices on par with first-growth Bordeaux wines. Queen Victoria was a loyal admirer, while a renowned German producer, Egon Müller, earned a Grand Prix at the 1900 Paris Exposition.

Riesling was Europe’s white-wine aristocracy. Then came 20th-century wars, industrialized farming, and a flood of Liebfraumilch, or mass-produced, cheap, and sweet wine, that dulled the grape’s reputation abroad. By the 1990s and early 2000s, quality Riesling had become more of a sommelier favorite than a mainstream success. Brilliant when made well, it was often overshadowed by widespread perceptions that German wine meant syrupy sweetness in a blue bottle.

Fortunately, that stereotype is collapsing. Riesling is undergoing a global renaissance, driven by shifting consumer tastes, ambitious producers, and evolving climates. 

The most profound change is this: the modern Riesling conversation is no longer dominated by sweetness. Dry, precise, terroir-expressive, and mineral-driven examples have taken center stage.

Germany Leads the Pivot

During the last two decades, producers in Germany, Riesling’s homeland, have been redefining the grape’s identity. While off-dry Kabinett, late-harvest Spätlese and Auslese, and noble sweet wines like Eiswein, Beerenauslese, and Trockenbeerenauslese remain treasured, Trocken (dry) styles now dominate domestic consumption and premium production.

A major turning point came in the early 2000s, when the Verband Deutscher Prädikatsweingüter (VDP) introduced Grosses Gewächs (GG), linking the country’s most prestigious vineyards to dry wines. This signaled that Riesling is capable of nuance, longevity, and true site expression, not merely a sugary curiosity. 

Climate change accelerated this shift. Warmer seasons raised sugar levels and lowered acidity, making balanced sweet wines harder to achieve while highlighting the appeal of crisp, mineral-driven dry styles.

These changes are noted on German wine labels, but, for some consumers, the terminology can be confusing. “Trocken” and “Halbtrocken” are straightforward terms that designate whether a bottle is dry or off-dry, respectively. However, Prädikat terms like “Kabinett,” “Spätlese,” and “Auslese” describe grape ripeness at harvest, not final sweetness. When “Trocken” accompanies these designations, it simply means the riper grapes were fermented dry. 

Another way to note whether a German Riesling is sweet or dry is to consider its alcohol level. Most dry Rieslings hover around 12% alcohol by volume (abv) or higher, while sweeter Prädikat wines often fall below 10% abv.

Riesling remains Germany’s most planted variety, spanning about 24,000 hectares. But more vineyards are now managed specifically for dry wine, focusing on lower yields, careful canopy work, earlier picking, and farming aimed at cultivating minerality rather than sugar accumulation.

Additionally, Germany’s flourishing natural wine scene reinforces the move toward dryness. With little to no added sulfur, and wines often bottled unfiltered, residual sugar poses a stability risk, potentially causing refermentation. 

Without sulfur to block malolactic fermentation, many natural Rieslings also undergo the chemical process that softens acidity. This further distinguishes them from the precise, high-acid GG style. As a result, most natural wine producers ferment fully dry, normalizing dryness among growers and consumers alike.

Riesling Expressions Around the World

Riesling’s versatility has always been its secret power. Late-ripening, naturally high in acidity, and exceptionally expressive, the grape adapts effortlessly across continents. As consumers embrace fresher, lower-alcohol, food-friendly whites, Riesling producers worldwide have responded with an emphasis on dry styles.

Alsace has long produced structured Rieslings that are predominantly dry today, and often have a sweetness scale on the back label. Locals sometimes describe the two styles in ways that reflect their own history and collective identities: the “Protestant” version is vertical, sharp and nuanced, and the “Catholic” style is broader, more expressive, and occasionally sweeter. The region’s patchwork of limestone, granite, and volcanic soils create wines that are powerful yet crystalline, showing citrus oil, white flowers, and a firm, savory backbone.

In Austria, particularly the Wachau, Kamptal, and Kremstal, Riesling is almost always dry, taut, and mineral. These wines have a broader palate weight than in Germany or Alsace, but the same emphasis on precision. The herbal lift, stone-fruit depth, and driving acidity makes these wines standout food partners.

In the United States, especially Washington State and New York’s Finger Lakes, Riesling occupies a stylistic middle ground. Washington Rieslings balance ripe peach and citrus with brisk acidity in both dry and off-dry styles. Bottles in the Finger Lakes tend toward delicacy: cool nights and slate soils yield bright, linear wines that range from bone dry to lightly sweet, all defined by finesse.

Australia’s Clare and Eden Valleys champion bone-dry styles bursting with lime, citrus, and saline verve, while New Zealand’s plantings have declined as producers shift toward other aromatic varieties. Slovenia, Northeast Italy, and parts of Austria are exploring skin-contact, orange-wine Rieslings, showcasing the grape’s elasticity. 

Sparkling Riesling is also resurging, especially in Germany, where it remains a distinctive delicacy.

How to Choose the Right Riesling for You

Choosing the right Riesling comes down to understanding its spectrum. From bone-dry, mineral-driven bottlings across Central Europe, the U.S., and Australia, to delicately off-dry styles from Germany and the Finger Lakes, to the richer expressions from Alsace, and the lusciously sweet wines worldwide that remain sought-after treasures, Riesling offers a style for every palate. It even excels in natural wine form, where its high acidity and structure make it one of the category’s most stable and compelling varieties.

As outdated stereotypes fade, the grape’s true identity emerges: a noble, adaptable variety that channels place with unmatched clarity. Whether you crave piercing acidity, a whisper of sweetness or something in between, there’s a Riesling out there with your name on it.

Here’s how to find it:

  • On labels, look for Trocken to guarantee dryness.
  • Below circa 11% abv may signal sweetness, while 11.5 to 14% typically means dry.
  • Kabinett can be dry or off-dry; Spätlese and Auslese often lean riper and sweeter unless explicitly labeled dry or Trocken. These are normally premium wines that are worth putting away in the cellar, while other off-dry styles are marketed for easy consumption.
  • The back label might have a sweetness scale which will point you in the right direction.
  • Alsace, Austria, Australia, and regions in the U.S. tend toward dry styles.
  • Sweet Rieslings, particularly late-harvest or botrytized wines, remain exceptional with spicy foods, blue cheese, charcuterie, or dessert.
  • For natural Rieslings, ask a local retailer to point you in the right direction. These wines tend to be lower in acidity but are still vibrant, fresh, and often rounder.

title: No Hong Kong Trip Is Complete Without a Visit to This Hotel Bar
summary:
Newly ranked #25 on this year's 50 Best Bars list, Four Seasons Hong Kong's Argo looks to its home city for inspiration.

The post No Hong Kong Trip Is Complete Without a Visit to This Hotel Bar appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Hong Kong is the kind of intercultural, intertemporal urban hub that lends itself to creative world-building. Thanks, in part, to its history as a former British colony, the city is simultaneously Eastern and Western, and both ancient and futuristic—a combination its tourism industry leads with in its campaigns.

For decades, it’s been an artistic bellwether, with local auteurs and directors like Wong Kar-wai taking inspiration from the city’s past and reinventing it in films like Chungking Express and In the Mood for Love. Of course, the region’s cuisine also blends traditional roots with newer influences, but it really needs no introduction: if you’ve ever indulged in dim sum or char siu pork, you’re already familiar with the allure of Cantonese food.

Hong Kong’s bar scene is no different. Due to the region’s softer tourism policies (compared to mainland China), visitors have been flocking to the bustling archipelago for both business and pleasure for decades, so much so that Hong Kong developed a reputation as being a haven for “drunk-expats,” as we highlight in a story in our November 2025 print issue.

That has since changed, however, as both recent political upheaval in the region and the Covid-19 pandemic sent large numbers of expats packing. What’s remained is a reexamination of the city’s future, and a rededication to the heritage of Hong Kong, itself—in its drinks scene and beyond.

A shining example of this shift lies in the neighborhood of Central, just steps from Victoria Harbour, at the Four Seasons Hotel Hong Kong’s flagship cocktail bar, Argo, and the world agrees—the bar ranked #25 on this year’s 50 Best Bars list.

The Decor

Walking into Argo feels like entering a conservatory set in the home of Jay Gatsby. Retro-style light fixtures hang from the ceiling, with terrariums and mirrors lining the walls that play with the abundant natural light streaming in through its massive windows (the Harbour view isn’t bad, either).

The balance between extravagance and warmth mirrors its Hong Kong backdrop. “When a guest walks into Argo for the first time, I want them to feel genuinely welcomed—not intimidated,” says Argo’s beverage manager, Jonathan Gabbay. “Hotel bars can sometimes come across as a bit too polished or exclusive. That’s never been the vibe we want.”

Argo’s pièce de résistance, however, is a towering, hauntingly beautiful bar structure, with backlit, shimmering shelves stocked with myriad spirits. It’s a mesmerizing centerpiece set in a perfect location—visible from the hotel lobby, the glimmering bar beckons to anyone who steps foot on the property.

The Drinks

Named for the ship Jason and his Argonauts helmed in their quest for the Golden Fleece, Argo and its menu seek to bring guests on a similar journey of discovery. Since he was named beverage manager in 2025, Gabbay’s mission has been to reshape the bar’s cocktail program into a “love letter to the city.” That mission now takes shape in Exploration—a new three-part menu that helped Argo achieve its #25 ranking on this year’s Best Bars list.

The menu’s first chapter, Local Encounters, looks to its home city for inspiration, crafting drinks in collaboration with local artisans, artists, and even a practitioner of Chinese medicine. A special shoutout goes to the Broth & Soul, a cocktail made in partnership with Big JJ Seafood Hotpot (a local spot with a cult following), which combines Grey Goose vodka, clarified tomato juice, and sherry infused with hotpot spices.

The next section is Seasonal Journeys, which, true to its name, shifts its focus to the seasonality and terroir of the region. Here, classic cocktails spotlight local ingredients, resulting in concoctions like the Floral Martini, which uses a tincture made from local flowers, and a Fruity Highball that combines Glenlivet 12 Y.O. with a fruit cordial and tea.

Finally, Exploration concludes with Timeless Passages, a selection of ten Argo favorites that have been captivating guests since the bar opened in 2021. The flagship Argo Martini employs the bar’s own Argo Gin, crafted with help from South Australia’s The Never Never Distilling Co.

The Crowd

Given its critical acclaim, as well as its Four Seasons Hong Kong setting (whose culinary and bar team currently maintain seven Michelin stars across the hotel’s Lung King Heen, Caprice, and Noi restaurants), expect to see both curious and in-the-know guests from all over the world. “Argo is for everyone. Every kind of drinker,” Gabbay says. “It’s a safe place and a sharing place. You don’t need to know the industry or speak the language of cocktail bars to belong here.”

Argo is open to the public, and accepts both walk-ins and reservations. For a more personalized experience, guests can also enjoy Argo’s Exploration menu in its private, botany-inspired Glass Room.

The Bottom Line

In Hong Kong, great cocktail options abound. And while the city is currently home to four of the world’s top 50 bars, according to 50 Best—including the #1 spot, Bar Leone—Argo’s dazzling interior and its commitment to Hong Kong craftsmanship make it stand out in a town full of standouts.

If you’re planning a trip to the region, make sure to check out our guide to Hong Kong’s electric bar scene, and don’t forget a stop at the Cathay Pacific lounges at Hong Kong International Airport—a wonderful drinks experience in itself, with bartenders whipping up classic cocktails, as well as the airline’s signature Cathay Delight mocktail, a blend of kiwi juice, whole milk, coconut milk, and mint leaves.

title: We Cracked the Code on a Low-ABV Margarita
summary:
Agave wine stars alongside lime juice, agave syrup, and orange juice in this low-alcohol spin on the classic margarita.

The post We Cracked the Code on a Low-ABV Margarita appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
In one of the most popular cocktails at Mediterranean restaurant Sipeos, which serves only beer, wine, and zero-proof cocktails, low-alcohol agave wine stands in for traditional tequila. “It’s balanced and you still taste the agave,” Piccione assures. “If you didn’t know it was low abv, you wouldn’t be able to tell.”

Agave wine, a sap extracted from blue agave that’s fermented with yeast and fortified with a small amount of an agave spirit, is growing increasingly popular in the United States. In this lower-abv margarita, the agave flavor “really shines through,” says Piccione.

Low-ABV Margarita Recipe

Courtesy of Vincenzo Piccione, bar manager, Sipeos, Walnut Creek, CA

Ingredients

  • 2 ounces Ola Sol agave wine
  • 1 ounce lime juice
  • ½ ounce agave syrup
  • ¼ ounce orange juice
  • Lime wedge, for garnish

Directions

Step 1
Combine all ingredients in a cocktail shaker with ice.
Step 2
Shake well.
Step 3
Strain into rocks glass over fresh ice. Garnish with lime wedge.
